LIME and Integrated Gradients provide complementary local and global attribution, helping validate whether high importance stems from spurious patterns. Sensitivity analysis confirms whether removing a feature changes prediction outcomes, isolating its causal or spurious role. Together, these tools identify features that are both shared and high-impact, even when semantically unrelated to the true class labels.

explanation.explanation: The model appears to have overrelied on these shared demographic features, which are strongly correlated with lower income in the training data due to co-occurrence patterns. The combination of 'Married-civ-spouse', 'Craft-repair', and 'Husband' creates a spurious signal that associates these values with <=50K, leading the model to incorrectly assign >50K when the true label is <=50K. This suggests data leakage from socioeconomic biases in the training data.

result.explanation: Both Instance A (13590) and Instance B (44018) share the same values for marital-status (Married-civ-spouse), occupation (Craft-repair), relationship (Husband), race (White), and sex (Male). These features are demographic and social attributes that are highly consistent across both instances. However, they are not strongly predictive of income level (>50K vs <=50K) when considered in isolation and are often overshadowed by more directly relevant features such as age, education-num, hours-per-week, and workclass. In correctly classified instances, these features tend to be less dominant or more variable, suggesting that the model may have overrelied on these shared demographic cues in the misclassified cases, leading to poor generalization. Since the true label for both is <=50K (correct label), the model incorrectly predicted >50K, possibly due to misweighting or insufficient learning from the informative features (e.g., age, education). Thus, these shared demographic features are not semantically meaningful for the prediction task and appear to have contributed to the misclassification.
